query: Earlier studies reported high hardness and compressive strength in AlCrCuFeNiTi, CuFeNiMnTi, and low-density AlCrFeTiX high-entropy alloys. However, some AlCrFeTiX alloys were brittle at 25 °C, and AlCrFeTiCo showed only 1.8% plastic strain at 600 °C. Because these findings concern different alloy systems, they do not explain the deformation behavior or the relatively low hardness and strength of equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its simple solid-solution state, despite its favorable plasticity and machinability. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs this combination of deformation, hardness, and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting alloy, state the composition, state, temperature, and loading limits of the hypothesis, identify the prior evidence supporting its premise, and specify results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In equimolar (CoCrFeNiTi) high-entropy alloys the governing parameter that couples low hardness and strength with high plasticity is their comparatively high intrinsic stacking-fault energy (SFE, > ≈40 mJ m⁻²).  The elevated SFE (set mainly by the high average valence-electron concentration generated by Co+Cr+Fe+Ni and only moderate Ti content) keeps Shockley partials closely bound, promotes ready cross-slip and dislocation climb, suppresses deformation twinning/ε-martensite formation and inhibits precipitation of hard ordered phases.  This produces easy dislocation glide, limited work-hardening and therefore moderate hardness/yield strength but large uniform strain and good machinability.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast and homogenised (1200 °C, 4 h, water-quenched) equiatomic Co-Cr-Fe-Ni-Ti single-phase fcc solid-solution bar, grain size 50–100 µm, negligible second phases.
generation.intervention: Reduce the alloy’s SFE by substituting 10 at.% of Ni with 10 at.% Al to obtain Co20Cr20Fe20Ni10Al10Ti20 (hereafter ‘Al-modified’).  All processing kept identical to the baseline to retain a single-phase fcc matrix (verify by XRD).
generation.conditions: Uniaxial tension and compression at 25 °C, strain-rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹; Vickers hardness at 9.8 N load; TEM at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Measured intrinsic SFE (e.g. weak-beam TEM) and the operative deformation substructures: (i) dissociated vs undissociated dislocations; (ii) twin/stacking-fault density; (iii) evidence of cross-slip versus planar slip bands.
generation.mechanism: Al lowers VEC and thereby the SFE.  A lower SFE increases partial separation and makes cross-slip difficult, leading to planar slip and nanotwinning.  These defects raise work-hardening and impede dislocation motion, boosting hardness and yield strength but reducing ductility.  Conversely, the high-SFE baseline alloy allows easy cross-slip, giving lower strength but greater plasticity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy, the Al-modified (lower-SFE) material will: 1) show ≥20 % lower SFE, 2) exhibit a >30 % rise in Vickers hardness and 0.2 % proof stress, 3) display strain-hardening exponents ≥50 % higher during tension, 4) achieve <15 % total elongation (≥50 % reduction versus baseline), and 5) contain plentiful deformation twins/stacking faults and pronounced planar slip with little cross-slip.
generation.baseline: Baseline CoCrFeNiTi: SFE ≈45 mJ m⁻² (estimated); Vickers hardness ≈200 HV; 0.2 % yield strength ≈250 MPa; uniform elongation ≥25–30 %; dislocation cell structure with frequent cross-slip and scarce twins.
generation.boundary: Prediction holds for 25 °C ≤ T ≤ 600 °C under quasi-static strain rates (10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹) provided the alloy remains single-phase fcc; not applicable if second-phase precipitation (>3 vol %) or if test temperatures are cryogenic (<150 K) where SFE decreases intrinsically.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative SFE values for multicomponent alloys are estimated; partial segregation of Al or formation of ordered B2 nanoprecipitates could contribute to strengthening, complicating attribution solely to SFE.  Magnitude of property changes may vary with grain size and processing.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two 20 mm × 5 mm × 2 mm dog-bone specimens: (i) baseline CoCrFeNiTi, (ii) Al-modified CoCrFeNi0.9Al0.1Ti, both homogenised identically.  (A) Measure SFE by weak-beam dark-field TEM fringe method and by synchrotron in-situ peak-broadening. (B) Record Vickers hardness (10 indents/sample). (C) Perform room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests to fracture with digital image correlation; extract 0.2 % yield stress, ultimate strength, uniform elongation and work-hardening rate. (D) Examine post-mortem TEM foils for twins, stacking faults, and cross-slip features.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if (i) Al-modified alloy fails to show a measurable SFE reduction OR (ii) despite reduced SFE, its hardness and yield strength do not increase by at least 15 % relative to baseline OR (iii) its uniform elongation does not decrease relative to baseline OR (iv) TEM reveals no increase in planar slip/twinning nor reduction of cross-slip.
